new_statements.translation_language: English glosses; Sebop forms in Blust's phonetic transcription
new_statements.rule_in_words: No prose rule exists. In Blust's 1971 citation-form transcriptions of Sebop (Long Loyang), every form that carries a stress mark has it on the final syllable, regardless of the penult vowel (u'tak, la'ka, pa'ray, ta'bat as well as pə'duk, mə'na); many forms are left unmarked. Read as: word stress final in citation forms (data-only, low confidence). Blust 2013: 186 warns, for Sarawak languages generally, that final stress in citation forms goes with penultimate stress in phrasal context and that stress is not phonemic anywhere in Borneo.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; unmarked forms on the same pages (e.g. p.107 ra?, diɓa?, laban, takən, tukat, uma; p.109 an lan, balu?, uaŋ, makay, jəp) could be unstressed-in-phrase or simply unmarked. Gemination after a short penult vowel noted: lamah '5' [lammah] (p.81), ma? [mma?] 'cooked rice' (p.91).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms elicited in the field (word level); no phrasal data marked for stress. Variety: Sebop of Long Loyang (Long Luyang), Tinjar, Baram basin, 1971.
new_statements.identity_note: The evidence is for Sebop of Long Loyang (= Long Luyang, Ethnologue dialect 'Long Luyang'; Blust 2017 'Long Luyang (Sebop)'; Smith 2017 'Sebop of Long Loyang'), upper Tinjar, Sarawak, speaker David Galang, 1971. Glottolog sebo1238 has no dialect nodes, so the entry is for the language. Do NOT transfer to Sebop the 'Long Wat' stress statements (Kroeger & Smith 2024; Smith 2020 AFLA handout; Blust 2013 vowel remarks): Long Wat is ISO [ttw] = Glottolog long1406 'Western Lowland Kenyah' (alt name Long Wat; dialect nucl1560 'Nuclear Long Wat'), a separate code renamed from 'Kenyah, Tutoh' by CR 2007-247; the main1275/kaya1334 check notes that equate Long Wat with Sebop are wrong (Blust 2017 fn.7 and Smith 2015/2017 treat Long Wat and Sebop as closely related but distinct isolects, 75% cognate). Kaipuleohone tags Blust's Long Ikang notebook section (RB2-003-C) as [sib], but Blust and Smith treat Long Ikang as Lebu' Vu' (long1406); Ethnologue lists 'Long Ekang' as a Sebop dialect. Sebop is also unrelated to the Sebop/'Sebob' entries in Glottolog's Penan references (Needham 2007, Sercombe 2006), which are Penan works.

sources.note: p.186: 'stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo.. many of the languages of coastal Sarawak, and some interior languages have final stress in citation forms, but penultimate stress in phrasal context. Final stress thus appears to serve as a marker of decontextualised lexical data.' p.183: Long San, Long Sela'an, Long Ikang (Lebu' Vu' = long1406) 'have final stress in citation forms'.
